role: Hiking footwear for hiking + repeated creek wading
model: Any old/thrifted trail running shoe (mesh upper, non-waterproof)
community_verdict: r/Ultralight and r/WildernessBackpacking consensus is that mesh trail runners that drain and dry fast beat boots for creek work; people who wade a lot just accept wet feet and dry out on the move rather than fighting to keep boots dry.
pros: free if already owned
no weight penalty vs boots
dries faster than any boot
cons: no ankle support
tread may be worn/slick on wet rock
no guarantee of fit
oct_ga_fit: BEGINNER CAUTION: fine for warm-ish days (50s-60s) with wool socks, but repeated wading in low-30s/40s creek water in non-insulated mesh trail runners risks cold feet/mild hypothermia for someone inexperienced with cold-water wading; a beginner should plan on wading boots/neoprene socks or accept wet feet only briefly and dry out fast near a fire, not as an all-day creek-panning shoe

community_verdict: Plastic pans in this class (Estwing BP-14, ASR Outdoor 14") are the standard cheap entry point recommended across TreasureNet/BladeForums threads for beginners — light, cheap, and the molded riffles work fine for learning technique before investing more.
pros: very cheap
lightweight for the backpack kit
black color shows gold well against contrast
cons: riffles are less refined than name-brand green pans — some fine gold can wash over them
less durable long-term than a purpose-engineered pan
oct_ga_fit: Perfectly fine starter pan for a group of first-timers learning technique
notes: Great for beginners; experienced members of the group may prefer the value-tier Garrett

role: Primary gold pan for hand panning
community_verdict: Cascade Prospecting's hands-on pan review and multiple TreasureNet threads name the Garrett Gravity Trap as the pan most serious hobby prospectors reach for — its industry-leading riffle design (30 years running) and bright green color for gold contrast make it the most-cited 'actually good' plastic pan on the market.
pros: sharper, deeper riffles retain more fine gold than generic pans
bright green improves gold visibility against black sand
virtually indestructible plastic, very light
cons: costs roughly double the cheapest option for a modest performance gain
oct_ga_fit: The pan most likely to actually catch Georgia's characteristically fine gold better than a generic pan
notes: This is the pan genuinely worth buying one of per person if budget allows even a small step up from bare-minimum

role: Primary gold pan for hand panning
model: 15" Super Sluice Gold Pan (two-stage riffle pan)
community_verdict: Cascade Prospecting's pan review names the Super Sluice its top overall pick, paired with a finishing pan for cleanup — its two-stage riffle system (coarse trap + fine trap) is built specifically for recovering the finest gold, which matches Georgia's reputation for fine flour/flake gold rather than nuggets.
pros: two-stage riffle system purpose-built for fine gold recovery
larger 15" size processes more material per pan
still light and unbreakable like other Garrett pans
cons: steeper learning curve than a simple traditional pan for total beginners
slightly heavier/bulkier for the backpack kit
oct_ga_fit: The best-performing pan for Georgia's fine gold, worth it for whoever in the group is most serious about maximizing recovery
notes: Give this one to the most experienced panner in the group; give beginners the simpler Garrett Gravity Trap or Estwing pan to learn on

role: Classifier for sizing material before/during panning
weight_note: per prior project sourcing (ASR 1/4" model confirmed $28.99, 1/2" comparable)
community_verdict: A single 1/2" or 1/4" coarse classifier is the standard starting recommendation across prospecting guides — screening out rocks and gravel before panning dramatically speeds up recovery, and one screen covers most Georgia creek gravel.
pros: cheap, effective first-stage screen
stackable with finer screens later if desired
cons: single mesh size means you still hand-sort some in-between material
oct_ga_fit: Sufficient for a first trip focused on learning technique in Georgia creek gravel
notes: Georgia gold tends to be fine — pairing this with a finer second screen (see value tier) meaningfully improves recovery

role: Classifier for sizing material before/during panning
community_verdict: Prospecting guides recommend a coarse-to-fine progression (1/2" then 1/4" then 1/8") to keep small screens from clogging with big rocks first — a stacked multi-mesh set is the commonly cited 'do it right' setup for anyone serious about maximizing recovery, especially for Georgia's characteristically fine gold.
pros: multi-stage screening captures more fine gold than a single mesh
nests together for compact packing
cons: more gear to carry/track than a single classifier
costs more upfront
oct_ga_fit: Strong fit given Georgia's reputation for fine gold — worth it for the group's shared base-camp cleanup station
notes: One shared set at the base-camp pan-out station, split 6 ways, rather than one per person

role: Classifier for sizing material before/during panning
model: Stainless Mesh Classifier Set incl. 50-mesh fine screen
community_verdict: Guides note that serious fine-gold prospectors go all the way down to 50-100 mesh screens to catch flour gold that would otherwise wash through a standard classifier — a stainless mesh set with a genuine fine screen is the recommended endgame setup for someone specifically chasing Georgia's fine gold rather than nuggets.
pros: stainless mesh far more durable than plastic screens
50-mesh fine screen catches gold a standard classifier set misses
cons: most expensive option, diminishing returns for a casual first trip
requires more cleanup technique to use the fine screen effectively
oct_ga_fit: Excellent if the goal is maximizing fine-gold recovery specifically; more setup than needed for a first casual trip

role: Snuffer bottle to suck up fine gold flakes from the pan

community_verdict: A basic plastic snuffer bottle is the standard, no-debate tool for picking flakes out of the pan without losing them in the swirl — prospecting guides describe it (or a turkey baster in a pinch) as an essential, cheap must-have.
pros: cheap, does the one job well
tiny and light
cons: plastic tip can crack/wear with heavy use
oct_ga_fit: All that's needed for a week of casual panning
notes: Buy 1-2 per person — cheap enough that losing one isn't a big deal

role: Snuffer bottle to suck up fine gold flakes from the pan

tweezers included cover larger flakes
cons: glass tip can chip if dropped on rock

role: Snuffer bottle to suck up fine gold flakes from the pan
used_price_range: n/a, cheap enough to buy new

won't degrade with repeated seasonal use
cons: marginal benefit over the value tier for a single trip

role: Crevice tools to pick gold out of bedrock cracks

community_verdict: A stainless set with an integrated magnet for pulling black sand/magnetite is a common step-up recommendation for cleanup efficiency — doesn't rust between uses and handles crevice work without dulling as fast as basic sets.

built-in magnet speeds up black-sand cleanup

role: Crevice tools to pick gold out of bedrock cracks

backed by an established prospecting brand
